Listen to this article Share Lagos State’s efforts to strengthen emergency response capacity are drawing attention to the need for stricter fire safety enforcement, regular inspections and improved prevention measures, as the state recorded 1,685 fire incidents resulting in 133 deaths and estimated property losses of N19.72 billion in 2025. The scale of the losses highlights the importance of identifying fire hazards before they escalate into emergencies, ensuring compliance with safety regulations and holding relevant parties accountable where negligence or non-compliance is established. The issue featured prominently at the premiere of Burning Point: Inside Lagos Fires, a documentary produced by CBI News, a subsidiary of Baywood Group, in Lagos on Monday, where government officials and stakeholders called for stronger collaboration on fire prevention, emergency preparedness and institutional accountability. Emperor Chris Baywood Ibe, founder and executive vice-chairman of Baywood Group, said fire safety should be treated not only as a public safety imperative but also as an economic priority and a critical component of sustainable development. He said the impact of fire outbreaks extended beyond fatalities and property damage to include destroyed business inventories, disrupted commercial activities, business closures and diminished community confidence. According to him, the challenge is not simply how emergency responders react when disasters occur, but how institutions and communities can reduce the frequency of incidents and prevent avoidable tragedies. Ibe raised questions about compliance with building and business safety standards, the effectiveness of regulatory enforcement, the availability of modern emergency equipment and the use of technology, early-warning systems and reliable emergency communications. He also stressed the need to examine whether lessons from previous fire incidents were translated into corrective action, measurable improvements and institutional accountability. “Journalism must do more than reporting the story. It must investigate why it happened, interrogate the systems and circumstances, establish indicative accountabilities and outline what can be done differently to achieve better outcomes in future,” he said. He said the documentary was intended to encourage evidence-based scrutiny of fire incidents and stimulate practical discussions on how to strengthen prevention, improve emergency response and address operational deficiencies. Ibe called for a coordinated approach involving government agencies, regulators, emergency services, property owners, businesses, civil society and the media, noting that effective fire disaster management required sustained investment in modern equipment, professional training, accessible emergency routes, regular safety inspections and public education. Meanwhile, Margaret Adeseye, director-general of the Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service, said the state government had procured 62 operational vehicles and recruited an additional 685 personnel between 2019 and 2023 to strengthen the agency’s emergency response capacity. Adeseye disclosed this in her keynote address at the event, explaining that the interventions also included expanded fire station coverage, the establishment of zonal headquarters, personnel training and the development of supporting infrastructure. She said the measures were necessary to meet the growing public safety demands of Lagos, given its expanding commercial, industrial, transportation and residential activities. According to her, the vehicles comprise fire engines, water tankers, rapid intervention vehicles, maintenance vehicles and hydraulic ladder platforms, which support firefighting, water supply, personnel mobilisation, equipment maintenance and specialised access during emergencies. However, she stressed that acquiring equipment must be matched with regular maintenance, proper deployment, adequate training and effective operational coordination. “The fundamental mandate of the Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service is to save lives and protect property,” she said. Adeseye identified firefighting, fire prevention, rescue operations and human resource development as the agency’s core responsibilities, emphasising that prevention remained essential to reducing casualties and economic losses. “The best fire incident is the one prevented,” she said. She added that the government had supported local and international training programmes to improve the technical competence and professional development of firefighters and rescue personnel. The director-general also highlighted the construction of a fire and mechanical engineering workshop to support fleet management, vehicle maintenance and operational readiness. She said the transformation of the Fire Service from a government department into a full-fledged agency represented an important institutional reform aimed at improving its capacity to respond to emergencies. Adeseye called for stronger collaboration among government agencies, businesses, property owners, professional bodies, communities and the media, stressing that public education, inspections and risk assessments were essential to identifying hazards before they resulted in injuries, deaths or property damage. She also advocated evidence-based scrutiny of fire incidents to establish their causes, determine whether preventive measures were in place and assess the effectiveness of emergency responses. According to her, findings from incident investigations should inform resource allocation, personnel training and improvements in prevention and response procedures. The Service reported that it rescued 473 victims alive and saved property valued at N118.32 billion in 2025, highlighting the importance of effective emergency response alongside preventive measures. Ibe urged stakeholders to move beyond general expressions of concern and develop specific recommendations on regulatory compliance, emergency response capacity, accountability and public awareness. He said the success of the initiative should ultimately be measured by the lives protected, losses prevented, systems strengthened and tragedies averted. The documentary premiere brought together government representatives, fire service officials, public safety professionals, business leaders and media practitioners to discuss ways of improving fire prevention and emergency preparedness in Lagos.
